$comment: The Secure Configuration Guide's single source (SCG-CSO-RSC, SCG-ENH-MRG). scripts/build-scg.py publishes it as /.well-known/secure-configuration-guide.json and .md; scripts/check-secure-config.py compares the live settings with `recommended` on every deploy (SCG-ENH-CMP/EXP). Changing a recommended default needs a new version and a changelog entry carrying the new defaults_sha256 (SCG-ENH-VRH); the builder and tests/test_secure_configuration.py fail otherwise. AI-drafted 2026-11-05 from the repository and read-only reads of the live account; for the operator's review.
title: Secure Configuration Guide: samaydlette.com
obtain_and_use: Obtain: the guide is public. Human-readable: https://samaydlette.com/.well-known/secure-configuration-guide.md. Machine-readable: https://samaydlette.com/.well-known/secure-configuration-guide.json, signed (secure-configuration-guide.bundle; verify with cosign verify-blob against the deploy workflow's identity, as https://samaydlette.com/trust/ shows). No account or request is needed.

Use: each setting names the account that operates it, the recommended value, why it matters, and the API or CLI call that reads and changes it. Compare a system's live values with `recommended`; the operator's own comparison, run on every deploy, is published at https://samaydlette.com/.well-known/security-settings.json (current values, the result per setting, and the decision record that covers any accepted deviation).

Change: every setting here is changed only through a reviewed pull request (Terraform for AWS resources, the repository settings for GitHub), never by hand in a console, except the root and owner settings that AWS and GitHub expose only to those accounts, which the operator applies and the deploy then checks.

accounts.name: AWS root user
accounts.how_named: The root user of the single AWS account that holds every production resource. It signs in with the account's email address, which is not published. AWS calls it the root user; this guide calls it aws-root.
accounts.access: Console only, with MFA, from the operator's own device. No access keys. Used only for the tasks AWS reserves to the root user (account settings, closing the account, restoring IAM administrator access); day-to-day work never uses it.
accounts.configure: The settings below under aws-root. AWS exposes the root user's own credentials (MFA device, access keys) only to the root user.
accounts.operate: Sign in only for a root-only task, finish it, and sign out. CloudTrail records every root sign-in and action in the account's management trail.
accounts.decommission: To retire the system: delete the deployed resources through Terraform, remove the root user's MFA device and any access keys, then close the account from the root user's account settings. Closing the account ends access for every IAM principal in it.

accounts.name: GitHub repository owner
accounts.how_named: The operator's personal GitHub account, which owns the repository sam-aydlette/samaydlette.com and so holds every repository and Actions setting, the environments and their reviewers, and the secrets.
accounts.access: github.com sign-in with two-factor authentication. Local git pushes go to branches, never to main; main changes only through pull requests that pass the required checks.
accounts.configure: The settings below under github-owner, in the repository's Settings (Branches, Environments, Actions, Code security).
accounts.operate: Review and merge pull requests; approve each production deploy in the prod environment. The deploy's checks re-read the environment and branch settings every run.
accounts.decommission: Transfer the repository with GitHub's transfer flow, or archive it. Before either, remove the AWS OIDC trust (infrastructure/bootstrap) so no workflow can assume an AWS role afterwards.

accounts.name: Operator IAM user
accounts.how_named: The one IAM user that belongs to the IAM group `operators`. It is the operator's day-to-day administrative identity (bootstrap applies, read-only verification). Its user name is not published; this guide calls it aws-operator-user.
accounts.access: AWS CLI with an access key; the user also has an MFA device, and no console password.
accounts.configure: Membership of the `operators` group gives its permissions; the settings below under aws-operator-user.
accounts.operate: Used for the bootstrap stack (applied by hand) and read-only checks. Production changes to the main stack go through the reviewed deploy, never this user.
accounts.decommission: Deactivate and delete its access keys, remove its MFA device and group membership, then delete the user.

accounts.name: CI roles (deploy, plan, nightly, package maintenance, incident reports)
accounts.how_named: Five IAM roles that GitHub Actions assumes through OIDC: the deploy role (aws_iam_role.deploy), the plan role (aws_iam_role.plan), the nightly evidence role (aws_iam_role.evidence_nightly), the package maintenance role (aws_iam_role.package_maintenance) and the incident reports role (aws_iam_role.incident_reports), all in infrastructure/bootstrap. No long-lived credential exists for any of them.
accounts.access: Only through GitHub's OIDC token, and only for the workflow subjects in each role's trust policy.
accounts.configure: infrastructure/bootstrap (operator-applied, reviewed). The settings below under ci-roles.
accounts.operate: The deploy role exists only inside an approved prod deploy; the plan role is read-only; the nightly role writes only .well-known/vdr-* objects; the package maintenance role writes only the certification package objects; the incident reports role writes only .well-known/incident-* objects.
accounts.decommission: Delete the roles and the OIDC provider from infrastructure/bootstrap and apply.

accounts.name: Silk Reeling user-pool administration
accounts.how_named: Administration of the Silk Reeling Cognito user pool (aws_cognito_user_pool.silk_reeling): creating users, and the pool's sign-in policy. Only the deploy role (through Terraform) and the operator user can administer it; app users cannot sign themselves up.
accounts.access: Through Terraform in the reviewed deploy, or the operator user's CLI for creating an app user.
accounts.configure: infrastructure/cognito.tf. The settings below under cognito-admin.
accounts.operate: Create an app user with `aws cognito-idp admin-create-user`; the user sets a password meeting the policy and enrolls TOTP MFA at first sign-in.
accounts.decommission: Delete the app users, then remove the pool from Terraform.

settings.setting: MFA on the root user
settings.implication: Without MFA, the root user's password alone controls the whole account, including closing it.
settings.change: Root user console: Security credentials, Assign MFA device.

settings.setting: Root user MFA is phishing-resistant (FIDO2 security key or passkey)
settings.implication: A TOTP code can be relayed by a phishing site in real time; a FIDO2 credential is bound to the AWS sign-in origin and cannot be.
settings.read: aws iam list-virtual-mfa-devices --assignment-status Assigned (a root entry means virtual TOTP)
settings.change: Root user console: Security credentials, Assign MFA device, Passkey or security key; then remove the virtual device.

settings.setting: Root user access keys
settings.implication: A root access key is an unrestricted, long-lived credential that no IAM policy can limit.
settings.change: Root user console: Security credentials, Access keys, Delete.

settings.setting: Account password policy for IAM users
settings.implication: Applies to any IAM user given a console password; weaker values make guessed or reused passwords work.

settings.setting: Account-level S3 Block Public Access
settings.implication: Stops any bucket in the account being made public by an ACL or bucket policy, whatever its own settings. The site is served through CloudFront's origin access control, never a public bucket.

settings.setting: IAM users other than the operator user hold no write permission and no console password
settings.implication: Every other IAM user is a read-only collector (an AWS read-only or SecurityAudit policy) or has no permissions and no credentials. A second user with write access would be an unreviewed administrative path.
settings.read: aws iam list-users; for each: list-groups-for-user, list-attached-user-policies, list-user-policies, get-login-profile
settings.change: aws iam detach-user-policy / remove-user-from-group / delete-login-profile (operator user)

settings.setting: The prod environment requires a reviewer before a deploy
settings.implication: Without a reviewer, a merged change would apply Terraform to production unattended.
settings.change: Repository Settings, Environments, prod, Required reviewers (or PUT /repos/{owner}/{repo}/environments/prod)

settings.setting: The evidence-nightly environment deploys only from main
settings.implication: The nightly role writes published evidence unattended; another branch must not be able to use it.
settings.change: Repository Settings, Environments, evidence-nightly, Deployment branches

settings.setting: main requires the four gate checks, for administrators too
settings.implication: These checks are the policy, test, scanner and change-classification gates; without them a change could reach main unchecked.

settings.setting: Two-factor authentication on the owner account, no classic personal access tokens
settings.implication: The owner account can change every setting above and the workflows that hold AWS trust.
settings.read: Not readable by any token the pipeline holds (GitHub exposes a user's two-factor setting and tokens only to that user). Stated once by the operator as a configuration fact (DEC-151); nothing recurs.
settings.change: github.com Settings, Password and authentication; Developer settings, Personal access tokens.

settings.setting: Every workflow declares its token permissions; none grants write-all
settings.implication: A workflow that declares its permissions never falls back to the repository's default token permissions, so the repository-level Actions setting (readable only by an administrator) governs nothing; write-all would give every step every write.
settings.read: The top-level permissions block of each file in .github/workflows/ (the repository the run checked out)
settings.change: Edit the workflow's permissions block, through a reviewed pull request

settings.setting: No repository ruleset lets anyone bypass it
settings.implication: A ruleset with bypass actors would let those actors skip the protections it adds; main's required checks are branch protection, compared above.

settings.setting: Dependabot alerts are enabled
settings.implication: Dependabot alerts are one of the detection feeds the vulnerability report reads; off, a known-vulnerable dependency raises no alert.
settings.read: GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/dependabot/alerts with the token the detection feeds use (403 means disabled)
settings.change: Repository Settings, Code security, Dependabot alerts

settings.setting: Dependabot version updates cover the Lambda's and the accessibility tool's npm packages, the GitHub Actions and the main Terraform stack
settings.implication: These are the dependency manifests in this repository that reach production or the pipeline; an entry removed stops update pull requests for it (docs/supply-chain.md).
settings.change: Edit .github/dependabot.yml, through a reviewed pull request

settings.setting: MFA on the operator user
settings.implication: The operator user can administer IAM; its access key alone must not be enough.

settings.setting: Operator user MFA is phishing-resistant (FIDO2 security key or passkey)
settings.implication: As for the root user: a TOTP code can be relayed by a phishing site; a FIDO2 credential cannot.
settings.read: aws iam list-virtual-mfa-devices --assignment-status Assigned (an entry for the user means virtual TOTP)
settings.change: IAM console: the user's Security credentials, Assign MFA device, Passkey or security key.

settings.setting: No console password on the operator user
settings.implication: The operator works from the CLI; a console password would add a second sign-in path to protect.
settings.read: aws iam get-login-profile --user-name <operator user> (NoSuchEntity means none)

settings.setting: At most one active access key, no older than 90 days
settings.implication: A long-lived key is the operator user's standing credential; rotating it every 90 days bounds the life of a leaked key.
settings.change: aws iam create-access-key, then update-access-key --status Inactive and delete-access-key for the old one

settings.setting: The deploy role trusts only this repository's prod environment
settings.implication: The prod environment requires a reviewer, so deploy credentials exist only inside an approved deploy.

settings.setting: The read-only plan role trusts only this repository's pull requests and main
settings.implication: Pull request runs get read-only credentials, never deploy permissions.

settings.setting: The nightly role trusts only this repository's evidence-nightly environment
settings.implication: The unattended write path stays limited to the one environment that deploys only from main.

settings.setting: The package maintenance role trusts only this repository's package-maintenance environment
settings.implication: The unattended package write path stays limited to the one environment that deploys only from main.

settings.setting: The incident reports role trusts only this repository's incident-reports environment
settings.implication: The unattended incident write path stays limited to the one environment that deploys only from main.

settings.setting: The package maintenance role may put exactly the certification package objects its workflow publishes
settings.implication: The unattended maintainer can write nothing else, and it can write every file it republishes, readable views included, so a run never fails half-published.
settings.read: aws iam get-role-policy (package-maintenance-publish; s3:PutObject resources, bucket removed)

settings.setting: Silk Reeling user pool: MFA required, admin-created users only, 14-character passwords with every character class
settings.implication: App users cannot sign themselves up, and every app user signs in with a strong password and TOTP MFA.

changes: First machine-readable release, replacing the prose guide in docs/policies.
Root and operator MFA stated as it is: virtual TOTP, an accepted deviation from the phishing-resistant default (DEC-150).
Deployer access-key rotation removed: CI uses OIDC roles and has no access key.
The retired Silk Reeling shared credential removed: app users sign in through Cognito with MFA.
Added the account-level settings, the operator user, the CI roles and the user-pool administration, each with the call that reads and changes it.
Added the repository settings the pipeline can read and now compares on every deploy and every night: workflow token permissions, rulesets, Dependabot alerts and Dependabot version updates.
The owner's two-factor setting is stated once as a configuration fact (DEC-151, amended); no recurring review.
Added the trust settings of the package maintenance and incident reports roles, compared on every deploy like the other CI roles.
Added the package maintenance role's write scope: exactly the objects its workflow publishes, the readable views included.
